AI translation, explained

An AI medical translator. A clear place in your workflow.

FluentCare resources3 min readPractical clinic workflows

In this guide

An illustrative workflow.
Follow your clinic’s approved policies.

An AI medical translator uses software to translate a conversation between languages. For a clinic team, the useful starting point is a specific communication task and a clear limit. FluentCare is designed for two-way voice translation in routine conversations. It does not connect you to a human interpreter, and a smooth demonstration does not establish clinical accuracy.

Try a fictional staff conversation

Imagine two colleagues practising appointment scheduling before evaluating a tool. One plays the receptionist; the other plays a visitor. They use an invented appointment, with no patient names, records or health details.

Give the exercise three simple steps:

  1. Choose the language. Check that the language you want to evaluate is available in the current release.
  2. Take turns. Say a short scheduling question, listen to the translated audio, then hear the reply. Leave room for each person to finish.
  3. Pause and review. Find the pause control, check whether both people can hear, and note anything that needs clarification.

This is an illustrative usability exercise, not a translated clinical script. It can show what your colleagues experienced with the controls and audio. It cannot prove that a language pair is accurate or suitable for patient use.

Know what the app is doing

FluentCare’s intended voice flow pairs English with a selected second language: speak, hear the translation, then hear the other speaker’s reply in English. Optional captions provide another way to follow the conversation. See the product overview for the visual walkthrough and clinic account model.

Keep the task clear when comparing tools. A spoken exchange, a translated document and a conversation with a qualified interpreter involve different kinds of support. AHRQ distinguishes spoken interpreting from written translation. A voice demonstration does not establish that a consent form has been appropriately translated.

Decide when to reach an interpreter

Your team needs an accessible interpreter process alongside any tool evaluation. AHRQ recommends planning language access in advance, asking about language preferences and training staff to reach interpreter support when unexpected needs arise. Our language-access workflow guide helps you organise that process.

AI translation can make mistakes. Use a qualified interpreter for informed consent, complex or high-stakes decisions, unresolved uncertainty, or whenever one is requested or required.

In the fictional scheduling exercise, agree on the next action if either colleague is uncertain: pause, clarify the task and follow your clinic’s approved support route. Do not treat a confident-sounding translation as confirmation that the other person understood.

Review privacy before patient use

FluentCare’s published privacy policy says to use non-patient information during release testing. Clinical language evaluation and provider healthcare/retention arrangements have not yet been verified for launch. Do not submit patient information until the applicable agreements and provider settings have been confirmed for your clinic.

The privacy and security overview explains the distinction between application storage and provider processing. Keep those questions in your review even when the interface feels straightforward. An easy demonstration does not answer an agreement or retention question.

Leave the test with a useful next step

Keep a short staff-test record: the fictional task, language selected, device used, whether both colleagues could hear, and any control or clarification problems. Record observations, not an accuracy score or a claim of clinical readiness.

Use our healthcare translation app evaluation guide to compare your requirements. Before moving further, confirm current release availability, evaluated languages and your clinic’s requirements. FluentCare’s get-started page shows the owner and staff routes and a way to ask about availability. Patients participate in the conversation; the current product model is built around clinic staff accounts.
